blocks.heading: What this section covers
blocks.text: Know the conventions of the forms the papers use and what each convention does for its reader; recognise an unseen text’s form from its features and say what those features are there to do.

blocks.heading: Form and conventions
blocks.text: Form is the kind of text a piece is, such as an article, a speech, an email or a review, together with the conventions its readers expect of that kind. Conventions are those expected features: a headline in an article, a salutation in a letter, a call to action in an advertisement. They are not decoration and they are not rules; they are the signals a reader uses to recognise what kind of thing is being read, so a writer can follow them or break them deliberately, and either choice means something.

blocks.heading: The forms the papers use
blocks.text: The forms the papers set are known by their conventions, and the list below names what is expected of them. An article carries a headline, a standfirst, a byline, quoted voices and short paragraphs. A speech addresses its audience directly, signposts its route, repeats key points so listeners can hold them and closes memorably. A formal letter and an email open with a salutation, state their purpose early and sign off. A blog uses a personal voice, direct address, headings and an invitation to respond. A review states what is reviewed, judges it against criteria, gives evidence and a verdict. A diary or a memoir writes in the first person and sets reflection beside events. A leaflet, brochure or advertisement uses headings, direct address, imperatives, benefits and a call to action. A report has a title, a stated purpose, findings in sections, recommendations and an impersonal register. A podcast or scripted talk keeps a host’s voice, spoken markers and signposting for listeners.

blocks.heading: Worked example: recognising a form
blocks.text: Take this opening, written for the purpose: "Dear Ms Shipanga, I am writing on behalf of the Ondangwa residents’ committee about the noise from the depot after dark." The layout is a message to one named reader, so it is a letter. The address — "Dear Ms Shipanga" — is direct and personal. The voice is a group speaking as one person, "on behalf of". The register is formal and public. The purpose is stated early: "about the noise". That evidence, from layout, address, voice, register and purpose together, gives one answer: a formal letter of complaint from a committee.

blocks.heading: Non-fiction that tells a story
blocks.text: Non-fiction is writing that presents itself as true: articles, memoirs, reviews, speeches, letters, travel writing. The boundary to watch is that non-fiction can use narrative techniques, such as scenes, characters and suspense, without becoming fiction, so a memoir extract that reads like a story is still a memoir, and the analysis says what its choices do for its reader.

blocks.heading: A form that announces itself
blocks.text: A leaflet opens: "Three ways to cut your water bill this dry season — inside." The heading promises a numbered list, so a reader who has thirty seconds at a kitchen counter expects to find it; the imperative "cut" and the possessive "your" put the reader in the sentence; the dash and the word "inside" withhold the answer, which is what makes the reader open the fold. Follow the conventions and the reader knows how to read it; the analysis then says what this leaflet does with them.

blocks.heading: When a convention is broken
blocks.text: A writer can break a convention on purpose, and the break carries meaning precisely because the reader expected the convention: a review with no verdict makes the reader supply it; a report that suddenly says "I" admits a person behind the findings, and the register shift is the point. In analysis, a broken convention is named as a choice like any other — what was expected, what came instead, and what the difference makes the reader notice.

blocks.heading: Naming is not analysing
blocks.text: The error to avoid is listing a form’s conventions as if the list were the analysis. A sentence that says an article "has a headline, subheadings and short paragraphs" has named three conventions and analysed nothing. The test is the job: every convention does a job for the reader, and a convention counts in an analysis only when the writer says what job it does for this reader. The headline of a feature article, for instance, teases rather than summarises, which suits a reader choosing what to read for pleasure.
